units: the writer of the message is taking a baking course
the mixture rises properly while it rests
the mixture sinks once it goes into the oven
the writer states that the instructions received were followed closely
the writer has tried a different raising agent
an experienced acquaintance puts forward an explanation
that explanation blames the fault on too much handling
the neighbour advises cutting the last rise short
the writer asks for a meeting before changing method
text: I am writing about the baking class you run in the community room. Since I joined, one problem has defeated me and I cannot work it out on my own. My dough rises beautifully while it rests, then sinks the moment it goes into the oven. I have followed your instructions to the letter, weighed out every ingredient, and even switched to a different raising agent. A neighbour of mine, who has been making bread since she was a girl, offered me an explanation. The dough is worked too hard, she says, and the structure holding it up gives way in the end. Her advice is to knead more gently and to cut the second rise short. I would rather hear your view before I try anything, since nobody knows the ovens in that room as you do. If you could spare me a few minutes after the next session, I should be very grateful.

units: the text sets two ways of cooking fish against each other
cooking over coals dries the surface and colours it
cooking with steam keeps the flesh moist
coals add a smoky aroma that the other method lacks
steam lets the clean smell of the food come through
cooking on a grill calls for a thin coating of fat
cooking under a lid needs no fat at all
firm flesh suits fierce heat better
delicate flesh falls apart and needs close watching
text: Should a fish go over the coals or into the steamer? The two methods stand less far apart than people assume, though they never end in the same dish. Coals dry the outside and colour it, and they drive the juices back into the flesh. Steam swells the fibres instead and holds the moisture where it is. What about flavour? Cooking over charcoal brings a smoky note that steaming will never produce, whereas steam lets the clean smell of the fish itself come through, with nothing laid over the top of it. And fat? The grill wants a thin coating, or the skin takes hold of the bars. Cooking under a lid asks for none at all. So which of them? Whichever suits the piece in hand. Firm flesh takes the flame well, while delicate flesh breaks up above boiling water and has to be watched closely.

units: a vegetable seller gives advice on cutting
he says the size of the cut changes with the plant
onion must be cut into thin slices so that it melts down
herbs are cut finely without being crushed
garlic is worked almost to a paste so that it spreads better
carrot is prepared either in shreds or in even dice
he advises against anything in between for that vegetable
he warns that a blunt blade damages the vegetables
he recommends sharpening the blade before a long session
text: You do not cut everything the same way, the man on the vegetable stall told me yesterday evening, over his crates. That, he reckons, is where most people go wrong. Onion has to be sliced very thin, otherwise it will never melt down properly in the pan. Herbs you cut with the very tip of the blade, lightly, never crushed, else they blacken and lose their scent altogether. Garlic he likes worked down almost to a paste, because only then does it spread right through the sauce. And carrots? He laughed at that one. Grate them, or cut them into perfectly even dice, but never anything in between. Then, as he handed me my change, he threw in one last piece of advice. A blunt blade bruises vegetables far worse than the clumsiest hand ever will, so put a proper edge on it before any long stretch of chopping, on a wet stone, and never in a rush.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping food comes long before any way of making cold
drying in the air was the first method
salt draws the water out of flesh and halts decay
smoke above a fire makes meat keep longer
smoked meat takes on a harsh taste
travelling traders carried these stores along long roads
distant kitchens took up identical methods
sinking meat in melted fat seals it away from the air
these methods live on in the recipes of today
text: Long before anyone could make cold, keeping food edible meant a running fight against damp and rot. The earliest cooks hung their catch in the wind to dry it out. Then came the discovery that salt pulls the water from flesh and stops decay in its tracks. Smoke followed. A joint left hanging over a fire took on a harsh, biting taste and would keep for whole seasons. Traders on the move carried such stores along steadily longer roads, until kitchens far apart from one another had settled on the very same methods. Later still, cooked meat was sunk in melted fat and sealed away from the air in a pot. Every one of those steps pushed back the day a food would turn, and every one has left a mark on the way we cook now, repeated by cooks who never stop to ask where it came from.

units: a pale foam appears on the surface of a cooking liquid
that foam comes from proteins freed by the heat
the particles set loose are too light to sink again
the bubbles carry those particles upwards
leaving the foam clouds the broth
a clouded broth turns grey and tastes heavier
the cook lifts it off with a ladle again and again
beating an egg white stretches those same proteins
the mesh that forms holds air
a trace of salt weakens the bonds and firms the foam
text: As the water begins to tremble in the pan, a pale foam climbs to the surface and clings to the sides. It is made of proteins that the heat has driven out of the food. Cooking loosens the fibres and frees particles too light to sink again, and the rising bubbles carry them up. Leave that foam where it is and it falls back into the broth and clouds it. The liquid greys, the taste turns heavy. This is why a careful cook lifts it away with a ladle, over and over, for as long as it keeps forming. Something close to it happens under the whisk. Beating an egg white draws those same proteins out into a supple mesh, and the mesh takes hold of the air. A pinch of salt hurries the whole thing along, since it weakens the bonds and lets the foam rise sooner, firmer and far steadier.

units: a fish stock carried a metallic bitterness
the cook first suspected an acid ingredient and then his pan
he went back through every step of his preparation
the bones had boiled for far too long
a short infusion with no rolling boil is what is needed
a long extraction sets sulphur compounds loose
the gelatine breaks down beyond that limit
he now rinses the bones and takes out the gills
he keeps the pan below boiling point
the stocks that come out are clear and free of bitterness
text: It began with a fish stock that gave off a metallic bitterness, the day before a service in a staff canteen. The cook blamed the vinegar first, then the pan he had used, and only afterwards went back through his own recipe step by step. The fault lay with the bones. He had let them boil for close to an hour, when a frame will stand nothing more than a short, barely moving infusion. Past that point the bones give up sulphur compounds and the gelatine breaks down. So he rewrote his method altogether. He now rinses the bones in cold water, pulls out the gills, brings the pan up short of boiling, and stops the extraction before the liquid ever heaves. A fine cloth strains the rest. Since that correction his stocks come out perfectly clear, the bitter note has gone, and his team report nothing amiss.

units: the recipe offers two implements for crushing herbs
the leaves must be washed dried and stripped of their stalks
with the mortar the salt and the garlic are crushed first
the leaves go in gradually and are not struck
the mortar gives a thicker and more fragrant texture
the colour holds better by that route
the electric device is used in short pulses
the bowl must be chilled so that heat does not cook the herbs
the oil goes in as a thin stream at the end
a dry cheese may be added in fine shreds
text: A herb paste may be made with a mortar or with an electric bowl, and the choice matters, since the two do not give the same texture. Begin by washing the leaves, drying them thoroughly, and stripping away the tough stalks. Working with the mortar, crush the salt and the garlic first, then add the leaves a handful at a time, turning the pestle rather than striking with it. The paste comes out thicker and more fragrant, and its colour holds far longer. Working with the electric bowl, use short pulses only, and chill the bowl beforehand, or the heat of the blades will cook the leaves and dull the whole preparation. Either way, pour the oil in at the end as a thin stream. A dry cheese may finally be grated over the top and folded in with a fork, lightly, until the paste is even.

units: a covered market has reopened after renovation work
the hall takes its light through the roof
the vegetable stalls now hold the middle ground
the fishmongers’ aisle has cooling that works without ice
part of the building is set aside for makers who process on site
a baker shapes his dough in front of the customers
a shared kitchen is offered to let by the hour
the traders approve of the ventilation and the drainage of water
those two faults used to bring repeated closures
future rents worry the sellers because the sum is not yet known
text: The covered market in the northern quarter reopened this week, after building work that ran almost a whole season. Visitors step first into a hall lit from the roof, where the vegetable stalls now hold the middle ground. Beyond them runs the fishmongers’ aisle, cooled in silence by a system that has done away with trays of melting ice. A third of the floor has gone to traders who process on the spot: a baker shaping dough in full view of his customers, a seasonal bottling bench, a cutting room. The management is also offering a shared kitchen, let by the hour, for caterers with no premises of their own. Stallholders praise the ventilation and the drainage, the two failings behind a string of earlier closures. What worries them is the rent, whose final level has still not been announced.

units: the steam stops you seeing as you come into the room
the fat melts in the bottom of the pot
the pieces of meat begin to brown at their edges
a smell of caramel signals that liquid must go in
the stuck juices are lifted off and the flame is turned down
a fragrant steam escapes from under the lid
that smell travels as far as the corridor
the sauce darkens and coats the spoon
the meat comes away with no effort
the heat is put out and the smell lingers in the house
text: You walk into the kitchen and you can hardly see a thing, the steam has taken over. At first the pot says nothing at all. It simply warms, the fat melts down in the bottom, the pieces of meat start to take colour round their edges. A little later comes a smell of burnt sugar, and that is your cue: in goes the liquid, up come the stuck bits off the base, down goes the flame. After that everything slows. The lid shivers, one bubble breaks, another follows, and a thick savoury steam works its way out through the gap and drifts as far as the corridor. Towards the end the sauce has darkened, it coats the back of the spoon, the meat gives way under a fork with no effort at all. Then you kill the heat, leave the pot alone under its lid, and the smell goes on filling the house until morning.

units: the writer refuses to treat home cooking as an optional pastime
where the handing down stops industrial food takes the room
the consequences show up later at the doctors
with no adult to pass it on the child never handles a blade
the child does not learn to judge when something is cooked
grown up he buys dishes that only need reheating
spending on food climbs
the range of foods eaten narrows
added sugar becomes the taste everything is measured against
the writer holds that the cost at school would be met by savings on care
text: We ought to stop treating home cooking as an optional pastime. Where the handing down of these skills stops, factory food moves into the gap, and the bill is read out later in the consulting room. The chain is almost mechanical. With no adult to pass on the order of the work, a child never picks up a blade, never tastes a dish halfway through, and never learns to judge when something is done. Left to himself as an adult, he buys what can be reheated, because that is the one route he knows. Spending on food climbs, the range on the plate collapses, and added sugar settles in as the taste against which everything else is measured. Making such workshops compulsory at school would cost a great deal, and nobody denies it. But the saving on long-term care would outstrip the bill, and the next generation would win back something it had lost.
